notes.bp: Clinicians must distinguish two voice disorders from patients' speech, but expert listening is scarce and subjective.
notes.wh: The disorders can sound similar and their acoustic signs vary across patients.
notes.naive: Rely only on a clinician's global impression or on generic acoustic features.
notes.ap: Combine expert-designed voice measures with representations learned directly from the waveform.
notes.mech: A CNN receives handcrafted features and self-supervised waveform representations and predicts ADSD versus pMTD on a newly collected patient dataset.
notes.math: The decision is a two-class prediction; accuracy measures the fraction of correctly classified patients.
notes.ww: The paper reports 83.3% classification accuracy.
notes.limits: The result is tied to the constructed dataset, its patient mix, and the two diagnoses; clinical deployment, calibration, and external validation remain open.
notes.title: Hybrid Expert Knowledge and Self-Supervised Learning for Diagnostic Modeling of Adductor Spasmodic and Primary Myotonic Dysphonia

notes.bp: A child ASR system must recognize speech when only a small amount of child data is available.
notes.wh: Children's voices differ from adults and scarce data makes both acoustic modeling and pronunciation variation difficult.
notes.naive: Train a standard spectrum-only ASR model and accept its data-scarcity error.
notes.ap: Augment in-domain data, add glottal-activity information to spectral features, and normalize features with fMLLR.
notes.mech: The study compares a baseline with augmented data, MFCCs plus glottal parameters, and fMLLR-normalized features.
notes.math: Character error rate is the main error measure; relative reduction compares each system with the baseline.
notes.ww: The combined normalized MFCC and glottal features give a reported 40% relative character-error-rate reduction over baseline.
notes.limits: The evidence is limited to the child's speech data and tested feature pipeline; languages, age ranges, and transfer to new schools or microphones are not established.
notes.title: On Enhancing the Performance of Children's ASR Task in Limited Data Scenario

notes.bp: A separator must recover each speaker while also coping with where speakers and microphones sit in a reverberant room.
notes.wh: Noise and reverberation can make room effects look like properties of the speech itself.
notes.naive: Ask one network to separate speech while treating the room and microphone arrangement as irrelevant nuisance.
notes.ap: Predict speech separation and the physical recording conditions together, then use curriculum learning to stabilize training.
notes.mech: SepVAC jointly estimates separated speech, speaker locations, microphone-array location, and room acoustic parameters on SMS-WSJ-Plus.
notes.math: Word error rate evaluates the usefulness of the separated signal to recognition; the multitask losses constrain both speech and scene estimates.
notes.ww: The paper reports a 0.67-point WER improvement over SpatialNet.
notes.limits: The result is author-reported on SMS-WSJ-Plus and its simulated acoustic conditions; real rooms, imperfect localization, and independent reproduction remain open.
notes.title: SepVAC: Multitask Learning of Speaker Separation, Speaker Localization, Microphone Array Localization, and Room Acoustic Parameter Estimation in Various Acoustic Conditions

notes.bp: In a group conversation, a listener's brain activity can indicate which talker they are attending to; the system should recover that talker's speech.
notes.wh: The neural cue is noisy and the extracted waveform can sound plausible while still losing the speech envelope that carries intelligibility.
notes.naive: Optimize only waveform reconstruction and hope the attended speaker remains identifiable.
notes.ap: Train the extractor on two linked targets: the target waveform and its amplitude envelope.
notes.mech: NeuroSpex+ uses EEG-derived reference cues and jointly predicts the target waveform and speech envelope to shape its mask.
notes.math: The two reconstruction objectives constrain both detailed waveform quality and slower envelope structure; signal-quality measures compare with baselines.
notes.ww: The paper reports significant improvement over baseline speaker-extraction systems.
notes.limits: The evidence is bounded to the recorded EEG/speech setup and tested mixtures; listener attention changes, clinical use, and independent reproduction remain open.
notes.title: NeuroSpex+: Dual-Task Training of Neuro-Guided Speaker Extraction with Speech Envelope and Waveform

notes.bp: Reverberation smears speech, and cochlear-implant users are especially affected; a useful enhancer must restore intelligibility, not just make the waveform look cleaner.
notes.wh: Transient speech cues can be blurred by room reflections and by the implant's representation of sound.
notes.naive: Use a fixed convolutional receptive field or optimize only for normal-hearing listeners.
notes.ap: Let deformable convolution move its receptive field to the distortion, and evaluate both signal measures and listeners with cochlear implants.
notes.mech: A deformable-convolution GAN is trained for dereverberation, first tested on REVERB and then assessed in listening tests with normal-hearing and CI users.
notes.math: The learned offsets change which neighboring time-frequency evidence is combined; intelligibility and quality are judged by objective tests and listener responses.
notes.ww: The paper reports markedly improved CI speech intelligibility by preserving envelope and transient structure.
notes.limits: The claim is bounded to REVERB conditions, the tested listeners, and the GAN configuration; broader hearing profiles, rooms, and independent replication remain open.
notes.title: A Deformable Convolution GAN Approach for Speech Dereverberation in Cochlear Implant Users

notes.bp: An ASR model should recognize non-native speech across several accents even when each accent has little labeled data and the accent is unknown at test time.
notes.wh: Accent changes sound patterns in different ways, and adapting to one accent can erase performance on others.
notes.naive: Fine-tune one shared model or train a separate full model for every accent.
notes.ap: Keep several small accent-specific adapters and let the system combine them, with or without knowing the accent.
notes.mech: MAS-LoRA attaches low-rank adapters specialized to accents to Whisper and evaluates known- and unknown-accent routing on L2-ARCTIC.
notes.math: Word error rate measures recognition; comparisons include ordinary LoRA, full fine-tuning, and forgetting after adaptation.
notes.ww: The paper reports lower WER than those baselines, stronger gains when the accent is known, and less catastrophic forgetting.
notes.limits: The result is tied to L2-ARCTIC, its accent set, Whisper, and routing assumptions; spontaneous speech and accents outside the corpus remain open.
notes.title: Mixture of LoRA Experts for Low-Resourced Multi-Accent Automatic Speech Recognition

notes.bp: Emotion recognition should work for languages with few labeled examples, not only for languages with large emotion datasets.
notes.wh: Emotion labels are scarce and expressive cues do not transfer unchanged across languages.
notes.naive: Train a supervised classifier only on the small labeled target-language set.
notes.ap: Learn a speech representation without labels using contrastive learning or BYOL, then transfer it across languages.
notes.mech: The study compares self-supervised objectives and analyzes their cross-lingual behavior for Urdu, German, and Bangla emotion recognition.
notes.math: F1 measures class decisions; the comparison asks how much it improves over supervised or conventional representation learning under limited labels.
notes.ww: The paper reports F1 improvements of 10.6% in Urdu, 15.2% in German, and 13.9% in Bangla.
notes.limits: The reported gains depend on the selected languages, labels, augmentations, and emotion definitions; cultural validity and transfer to new languages remain open.
notes.title: Learning More with Less: Self-Supervised Approaches forLow-Resource Speech Emotion Recognition

notes.bp: A deployed ASR system must keep learning as new languages and domains arrive in an uneven real-world stream.
notes.wh: A model can learn the new episode while forgetting older languages, and simulated episodes hide irregular shifts.
notes.naive: Shuffle all data together or evaluate continual learning on artificially regular episodes.
notes.ap: Measure language-incremental, domain-incremental, and joint language-plus-domain learning on naturally arriving speech.
notes.mech: NIRANTAR contains 3,250 hours from 22 languages and 208 Indian districts, with non-uniform episodes and human transcripts; existing continual-learning methods are compared.
notes.math: The central objects are recognition error over time and retention after each episode; the framework separates language and domain changes instead of averaging them away.
notes.ww: The paper finds that no single evaluated method performs consistently across the three scenarios.
notes.limits: This is a benchmark and comparative study, not proof that one method is universally best; the geography, languages, episode order, and ASR models define the boundary.
notes.title: NIRANTAR: Continual Learning with New Languages and Domains on Real-world Speech Data

notes.bp: People who speak Igbo, Hausa, or Yoruba need speech technology trained on enough varied speech to work beyond a few speakers.
notes.wh: African languages are underrepresented, and small or homogeneous datasets cannot expose speaker, accent, and recording variation.
notes.naive: Reuse large-resource-language data or build a small dataset without measuring its diversity.
notes.ap: Collect a large, culturally grounded speech-text corpus and test whether it improves several ASR families.
notes.mech: NaijaVoices contains 1,800 hours from more than 5,000 speakers; the paper analyzes acoustic diversity and fine-tunes Whisper, MMS, and XLSR.
notes.math: Word error rate compares models before and after the new data; corpus scale and speaker diversity are part of the intervention.
notes.ww: The paper reports average WER improvements of 75.86% for Whisper, 52.06% for MMS, and 42.33% for XLSR.
notes.limits: The corpus languages, collection process, transcription policy, and model choices bound the result; coverage of other African languages and deployment conditions remains open.
notes.title: The NaijaVoices Dataset: Cultivating Large-Scale, High-Quality, Culturally-Rich Speech Data for African Languages

notes.bp: Therapy and feedback need to know where a dysfluency begins and ends, not only whether an entire utterance contains one.
notes.wh: Only weak utterance labels are common, while real dysfluency boundaries are uncertain and synthetic timing is unrealistic.
notes.naive: Classify each utterance or trust every weak label as if it gave exact frame boundaries.
notes.ap: Turn overlapping speech windows into a graph, use a weakly trained classifier to refine links, and reduce its influence when it is uncertain.
notes.mech: StutterCut uses uncertainty-guided normalized cuts and adds frame-level boundaries for four dysfluency types to FluencyBank.
notes.math: Graph partitioning separates regions; Monte Carlo dropout estimates uncertainty, and F1 plus onset error measure segmentation quality.
notes.ww: The paper reports higher F1 and more precise stuttering-onset detection on real and synthetic data.
notes.limits: The evidence is bounded to FluencyBank, four dysfluency types, annotation quality, and the tested uncertainty model; therapy outcomes and new speakers remain open.
notes.title: StutterCut: Uncertainty-Guided Normalised Cut for Dysfluency Segmentation

notes.bp: A listener's short responses—such as agreement, continuation, or surprise—help a spoken dialogue feel responsive; a system should choose the right surface form without storing private speaker IDs.
notes.wh: Three broad classes are too coarse for generation, while identity embeddings are difficult to deploy and raise privacy concerns.
notes.naive: Predict a coarse backchannel class from a detailed speaker/listener identity embedding.
notes.ap: Replace identity-specific inputs with general speaker and listener embeddings and predict eleven surface-form categories as well as three classes.
notes.mech: The model uses speech, text, and general embeddings and compares three- and eleven-category prediction against ID-based systems.
notes.math: Accuracy is reported separately for coarse and fine categories, exposing the cost of richer response choices.
notes.ww: The paper reports 1.3% accuracy improvement for three classes and 0.9% for eleven classes over conventional ID embeddings.
notes.limits: The result is author-reported for the tested dialogue corpus and categories; natural turn timing, privacy leakage in embeddings, and user experience remain open.
notes.title: Backchannel prediction for natural spoken dialog systems  using general speaker and listener information

notes.bp: A retrieval system should find the right audio for a long, complicated text request, not only match short captions to short clips.
notes.wh: Audio and text embeddings are trained in different modalities, and simple CLAP-style matching weakens on long or compositional queries.
notes.naive: Use a fixed audio-text contrastive model and rely on its pooled embedding for every query.
notes.ap: Adapt a multimodal language model to produce a universal embedding, using prompts and text-pair training without requiring paired audio in the final training stage.
notes.mech: Vela uses selected prompts and in-context examples, then trains on text pairs; retrieval is tested on ordinary and newly designed long/complex benchmarks.
notes.math: Text-audio retrieval metrics compare the rank of the correct audio; the new tests ask whether the embedding preserves multiple pieces of a query.
notes.ww: The paper reports that Vela outperforms traditional CLAP models and is more robust on long, complex retrieval tasks.
notes.limits: The abstract says code is forthcoming and the result is tied to the chosen benchmarks and prompts; open-world audio, speech-specific retrieval, and independent reproduction remain open.
notes.title: Vela: Scalable Embeddings with Voice Large Language Models for Multimodal Retrieval

notes.bp: Emotion is ordered: a voice can be more or less excited or positive, but ordinary audio-text contrastive training treats labels as unrelated names.
notes.wh: Ignoring order loses gradual differences and leaves audio and language representations poorly aligned.
notes.naive: Pull each audio sample toward its text label while treating every other label as equally wrong.
notes.ap: Use valence-arousal rankings in a Rank-N-Contrast objective so nearby and distant emotional examples exert different forces.
notes.mech: EmotionRankCLAP aligns emotional speech with natural-language speaking-style prompts and contrasts examples according to their position in valence-arousal space.
notes.math: The loss encodes an ordering rather than only class identity; cross-modal retrieval tests whether the learned space preserves emotion relations.
notes.ww: The paper reports better emotion ordinality than existing emotion-CLAP systems on cross-modal retrieval.
notes.limits: The result depends on rating dimensions, prompt wording, and the tested emotion corpus; listener disagreement and transfer across cultures remain open.
notes.title: EmotionRankCLAP: Bridging Natural Language Speaking Styles and Ordinal Speech Emotion via Rank-N-Contrast

notes.bp: A speech codec should preserve what was said while allowing a system to change how forcefully it was spoken, such as neutral versus Lombard speech in noise.
notes.wh: Content, speaker identity, and vocal effort are mixed in ordinary representations, so changing effort can damage words or voice quality.
notes.naive: Use one undifferentiated code and hope a conversion model learns effort implicitly.
notes.ap: Place vocal effort in a designated codec layer while keeping semantic content in another layer, making effort controllable.
notes.mech: LombardTokenizer conditions the second quantization layer of SpeechTokenizer on vocal-effort encoders and tests neutral/Lombard conversion and synthesis quality.
notes.math: Layer-wise discrete codes represent different information; conversion metrics and quality tests compare effort control, intelligibility, and naturalness.
notes.ww: The paper reports better neutral-to-Lombard and Lombard-to-neutral conversion than existing methods while retaining synthesis quality.
notes.limits: The result is tied to the AVID/Lombard data, selected effort conditions, and codec; other speaking styles, languages, and independent listening tests remain open.
notes.title: LombardTokenizer: Disentanglement and Control of Vocal Effort in a Neural Speech Codec

notes.bp: An anonymizer must hide who is speaking while keeping the words and useful speech intact; a strong attacker may exploit prosody rather than obvious voice quality.
notes.wh: Speaker identity leaks through phone duration and pitch variation even after voice conversion, and a single recognition score does not reveal the leak.
notes.naive: Convert the voice and assume identity is removed once the main spectral cues change.
notes.ap: Add interpretable controls that alter phone duration and pitch variation, then test which changes defeat the speaker-recognition attack.
notes.mech: Private kNN-VC extends kNN voice conversion with duration and variation anonymization and compares target-selection strategies under an attack protocol.
notes.math: Privacy is measured through attacker recognition error; the interpretable factors connect a score change to a specific speech property.
notes.ww: The paper reports that anonymizing duration and variation substantially increases privacy and that target selection changes attack outcomes.
notes.limits: The evidence is bounded to kNN-VC, the attack model, selected prosodic factors, and utility measures; stronger attackers and human judgments remain open.
notes.title: Private kNN-VC: Interpretable Anonymization of Converted Speech

notes.bp: A text-to-speech system should sound natural when a speaker mixes languages in one utterance, as people commonly do in multilingual communities.
notes.wh: Monolingual training assumptions make language switches, pronunciation, and voice continuity brittle.
notes.naive: Force the input into one language or fine-tune on a new code-mixed dataset.
notes.ap: Infer code-mixed speech from multilingual text without requiring additional training data or fine-tuning.
notes.mech: The proposed inference procedure sends multilingual input through an existing TTS system and evaluates generated code-mixed speech with automated MOS-style measures.
notes.math: The central tradeoff is whether language-switch content is retained while synthesized audio remains natural; the paper uses automated quality scoring rather than a new training loss.
notes.ww: The paper reports an approach for code-mix inference without extra data or fine-tuning; the preserved evidence does not establish broad human preference gains.
notes.limits: The paper's method and evaluation details are bounded by the selected TTS system, languages, and automated metric; human listening, pronunciation accuracy, and unseen language pairs remain open.
notes.title: Code Mix TTS: An Approach to Infer Human Like Speech for Multi-Lingual Input Texts

notes.bp: A depression detector trained in one recording setting should remain useful when test speech comes from another environment, demographic mix, or dataset.
notes.wh: Noise, gender, age, and collection procedures change the speech distribution without changing the clinical question.
notes.naive: Train once on a clean source dataset and assume the test distribution is the same.
notes.ap: Adapt the model at test time using the incoming unlabeled speech so its internal features respond to the new distribution.
notes.mech: The study applies test-time training to a speech-based depression detector and tests shifts from noise, gender, and dataset/curation differences.
notes.math: Performance under each shift is compared before and after adaptation; the important object is the distribution gap, not only the average source score.
notes.ww: The paper reports substantial performance improvement under the tested shifts.
notes.limits: The task is a clinical screening proxy, not a diagnosis; adaptation stability, labels in deployment, privacy, and external clinical validation remain open.
notes.title: Test-Time Training for Speech-based Depression Detection

notes.bp: Generative speech codecs need listening tests sensitive enough to detect subtle artifacts, but expert MUSHRA studies are expensive and objective metrics can mis-rank new systems.
notes.wh: Crowdsourced listeners vary by platform and expertise, while traditional metrics were designed for older signal distortions.
notes.naive: Use only objective metrics during development or reserve all listening tests for experts at the end.
notes.ap: Adapt MUSHRA for non-experts online, compare platforms with expert data, and test whether objective metrics agree with people.
notes.mech: The paper compares MTurk, Prolific, and expert ratings, measures test-retest reliability, and evaluates six objective metrics on generative speech codecs.
notes.math: MUSHRA ratings, reliability, platform effects, and metric-to-human alignment are separate quantities; collapsing them into one score hides the evaluation problem.
notes.ww: The paper reports platform-specific bias, reasonable crowdsourced comparisons under its protocol, and that traditional metrics undervalue generative models.
notes.limits: The result is bounded to the codecs, platforms, listener recruitment, and six metrics tested; other populations and model families remain open.
notes.title: Crowdsourcing MUSHRA Tests in the Age of Generative Speech Technologies: A Comparative Analysis of Subjective and Objective Testing Methods

notes.bp: A deepfake detector should face manipulations that fool people, especially when only a few speech segments are changed to alter meaning.
notes.wh: Many benchmark fakes are easier for humans to spot than real attacks, and scanning every frame wastes computation.
notes.naive: Train on broad synthetic fakes and inspect the whole recording uniformly.
notes.ap: Use language reasoning to choose critical phoneme segments for manipulation, then detect those regions with an adaptive two-level model.
notes.mech: PhonemeFake creates segmental manipulations, measures human and benchmark deception, and trains a detector that allocates computation to suspicious regions across three datasets.
notes.math: Equal error rate measures detection, localization checks whether manipulated regions are found, and speed measures the cost of adaptive processing.
notes.ww: The paper reports up to 42% lower human perception and 94% lower benchmark accuracy for attacks; its detector reports 91% EER reduction and up to 90% speed-up.
notes.limits: These are author-reported results tied to attack construction, datasets, detector thresholds, and the chosen language reasoning; unseen generators and adversarial adaptation remain open.
notes.title: PhonemeFake: Redefining Deepfake Realism with Language-Driven Segmental Manipulation and Adaptive Bilevel Detection

notes.bp: A speech-quality score should say not only that an utterance is poor but whether noise, coloration, discontinuity, or loudness caused the problem.
notes.wh: A single mean-opinion score hides different defects and cannot express uncertainty or relationships among them.
notes.naive: Predict MOS alone with a point estimator.
notes.ap: Model MOS and four diagnostic quality dimensions jointly as a multivariate probability distribution.
notes.mech: The model predicts a multivariate Gaussian through Cholesky factors and extends probabilistic affine transformations on NISQA ratings.
notes.math: The mean gives a point estimate, covariance gives uncertainty and correlations, and the NISQA dimensions provide a structured target instead of one scalar.
notes.ww: The paper reports state-of-the-art-level point estimation while uniquely providing uncertainty and cross-dimension correlation estimates.
notes.limits: The result is bounded to NISQA's labels and distributional assumptions; whether listeners and engineers benefit in new codecs or languages remains open.
notes.title: Multivariate Probabilistic Assessment of Speech Quality

notes.bp: A person with dysarthria may know what they want to say but be hard to understand; conversion should improve intelligibility without erasing useful content or identity.
notes.wh: Dysarthric speech varies by speaker and severity, and mel-spectrogram targets may make generation slow or blur the relevant units.
notes.naive: Map dysarthric mel features to clean speech with an autoregressive or speaker-specific generator.
notes.ap: Use discrete self-supervised acoustic units and conditional flow matching with a non-autoregressive Diffusion Transformer to map impaired to clearer speech.
notes.mech: The study compares mel-spectrogram and quantized SSL features, controls the output voice with WavLM-derived information, and evaluates generated speech for dysarthric intelligibility.
notes.math: The learned flow maps a conditioning representation to clean-speech acoustics; intelligibility and convergence compare feature choices and generation paths.
notes.ww: The paper reports that discrete acoustic units improve intelligibility and converge faster than the mel-spectrogram alternative.
notes.limits: The result is bounded to the speakers, severity range, target voice, and tested listening/evaluation protocol; naturalness, identity preservation, and clinical benefit remain open.
notes.title: Improved Intelligibility of Dysarthric Speech using Conditional Flow Matching

notes.bp: A large speech model must fit on practical hardware without losing recognition quality, especially when storage and memory are tight.
notes.wh: Below eight bits, transformer weight outliers make uniform quantization damage a small number of important parameters.
notes.naive: Round every weight to the same low-precision grid.
notes.ap: Cluster weights nonlinearly, allocate more bits to columns with many outliers, and retain only critical outliers in sparse FP32 form.
notes.mech: The method quantizes Whisper-Large-V3 after training and compares mixed precision and outlier retention across speech datasets.
notes.math: Bits per parameter expresses storage; WER measures recognition loss, and the columnwise allocation ties precision to the observed weight distribution.
notes.ww: The paper reports 2.12-bit quantization with a 0.17 percentage-point WER increase on LibriSpeech test-clean and under 1% degradation across additional datasets.
notes.limits: The result is author-reported for Whisper-Large-V3 and tested corpora; latency, energy, hardware kernels, and other model families remain open.
notes.title: Ultra-Low Bit Post-Training Quantization of Large Speech Models via K-Means Clustering and Mixed Precision Allocation

notes.bp: A speaker recognizer should recognize a person years later or in a different emotional state, while rejecting unknown people in an open set.
notes.wh: Age and emotion change the same speaker's voice, and limited enrollment data makes it hard to learn every future condition.
notes.naive: Enroll one fixed embedding and set a threshold that assumes the speaker is stable.
notes.ap: Use few-shot foundation-model tuning at enrollment and generate style-rich synthetic speech to expose time-varying and emotional conditions, with losses focused on unknown outliers.
notes.mech: The framework selects synthetic speech, tunes the foundation model with few enrollment examples, and evaluates open-set identification across time-varying and emotional benchmarks.
notes.math: Identification accuracy and open-set outlier behavior separate recognizing enrolled speakers from rejecting unknown speakers.
notes.ww: The paper reports stronger generalization to aging and emotional variation while maintaining resistance to unknown outliers.
notes.limits: The claim is bounded to the synthetic-data choices, foundation model, enrollment protocol, and benchmarks; real aging trajectories, spoofing attacks, and fairness across groups remain open.
notes.title: Towards Robust Speaker Recognition against Intrinsic Variation with Foundation Model Few-shot Tuning and Effective Speech Synthesis

notes.bp: An ASR and speech-translation system should preserve what a dialect speaker said rather than silently rewrite dialect grammar into the standard variety.
notes.wh: Dialect differences affect words, grammar, pronunciation, and what counts as a correct transcription; a single standard reference hides these distinctions.
notes.naive: Evaluate one multilingual ASR model against only a standardized transcript.
notes.ap: Create paired dialectal and Standard German references across three underrepresented dialect groups and compare model outputs against both.
notes.mech: Betthupferl contains four hours of read speech from Franconian, Bavarian, and Alemannic speakers plus Standard German; multilingual ASR models are evaluated for transcription and translation.
notes.math: Error analysis compares similarity to dialectal versus standardized references and inspects grammatical normalization, not only one aggregate score.
notes.ww: The paper reports model-dependent differences: the best system sometimes normalizes dialect grammar but often stays closer to dialect constructions.
notes.limits: The dataset is four hours of read speech from Southeast Germany; spontaneous speech, other dialects, conversational translation, and community judgments remain open.
notes.title: A Multi-Dialectal Dataset for German Dialect ASR and Dialect-to-Standard Speech Translation
